The thesis that mathematical objects possess a form of objectivity independent of human psychological or social construction receives direct support from the structure of scientific confirmation and the character of mathematical practice. The indispensability argument establishes that our best scientific theories quantify over mathematical entities and are confirmed by the empirical success of those theories; the scientific realist who accepts electrons on the basis of theoretical indispensability has no principled grounds for rejecting the existence of mathematical objects on similar grounds. This commitment arises because the very same standards of theoretical utility and predictive success that justify belief in unobservable physical entities apply without remainder to the numerical and set-theoretic apparatus required by those theories, rendering any selective skepticism about mathematical ontology arbitrary.

The phenomenology of mathematical discovery further indicates that these entities are encountered rather than projected. Mathematicians encountering unexpected theorems, failed proofs corrected by necessity rather than convention, and surprising connections across independently developed branches find their experience more naturally described as exploration of a domain with determinate structure than as invention of arbitrary formal systems. The sense of constraint that accompanies the correction of an invalid step or the recognition of a deep isomorphism between distant areas of research reflects responsiveness to features already present in the subject matter, features whose stability and independence from individual preference or communal agreement are precisely what allow such discoveries to accumulate across generations.

Nominalist alternatives that attempt to eliminate mathematical objects in favor of physical inscriptions or mental constructions face decisive technical objections: they either fail to recover the full expressive power of standard mathematics or generate circularity by presupposing mathematical structure in the account meant to eliminate it. Reductions that treat numbers as concrete tokens cannot encode the full range of impredicative definitions and transfinite reasoning without covertly reintroducing the very abstract resources they seek to avoid, while psychologistic versions that locate mathematics in mental constructions must already presuppose the coherence of infinite totalities or recursive functions in order to describe those constructions, thereby rendering the elimination incomplete and self-undermining.

The replication crisis in psychology is often framed as a story about methodological sloppiness, as if a generation of researchers simply forgot the principles of good statistical practice. This framing is diagnostically misleading. The methodological failures that have hollowed out the empirical literature are better understood as rational adaptations to an institutional environment that systematically rewards certain research behaviors and punishes others. The crisis is not fundamentally about what researchers do not know; it is about what the structure of academic incentives induces them to do, and about why the mechanisms ostensibly designed to catch such behaviors fail to do so. Correcting it therefore requires not better pedagogy but a restructuring of the field-level rules under which researchers operate.

Consider first the specific methodological pathologies that generated the crisis: underpowered studies with small samples, p-hacking through flexible choices in exclusion criteria and analytical specifications, HARKing by presenting post hoc hypotheses as though they had been predicted in advance, and selective reporting of outcomes that reached statistical significance while quietly abandoning those that did not. It would be a mistake to attribute these practices primarily to incompetence, because the researchers who engage in them are typically well-trained and perfectly capable of understanding why such practices inflate false-positive rates. The practices persist because they are instrumentally rational given the incentive structure in which careers are built. Journals disproportionately publish novel, positive, surprising findings; hiring and promotion committees count publications in high-impact outlets; grant agencies reward productivity measured in such publications. Within this environment, a researcher who runs adequately powered studies, pre-specifies analyses, reports null results, and devotes effort to replicating existing work will produce fewer publishable units than a competitor willing to exploit analytical flexibility. The behavior that erodes the literature is the behavior that the system selects for, and researchers who refuse to engage in it face genuine professional costs. Characterizing the problem as individual moral or technical failure thus mistakes the symptom for the cause.

The peer review system, which is often invoked as the quality-control mechanism that ought to prevent such problems, is structurally incapable of catching them under its current operating conditions. Reviewers typically see only a manuscript, not the underlying data, the analysis code, or any record of what the researchers had originally planned to do before seeing the results. They cannot therefore distinguish a hypothesis that was genuinely predicted from one that was constructed after the data were examined, nor can they identify which of many possible analytical specifications was chosen because it produced the preferred result. Peer review does not require pre-registration, does not mandate data sharing, and almost never involves independent replication of the reported analyses, let alone the reported experiments. Compounding these structural omissions, reviewers work under severe time constraints, typically unpaid and performing review as a marginal activity alongside their own research obligations. Even a conscientious reviewer, given a few hours and a polished narrative, cannot reconstruct the garden of forking paths that led to the reported result. The flexible analytical choices that most inflate false-positive rates are precisely the choices that leave no trace in a finished manuscript, and peer review as currently practiced is blind to them by design.

What is required, then, are interventions at the level of field-wide rules rather than at the level of individual virtue, and the shape of such interventions is reasonably clear. Pre-registration of hypotheses and analysis plans removes the flexibility that enables HARKing and p-hacking by committing researchers to their predictions before they see the data. Registered reports extend this logic by moving peer review to the stage before data collection, so that publication is contingent on the quality of the question and the method rather than the direction of the result, which eliminates the publication bias that drives selective reporting. Open data requirements make analytical choices auditable and permit independent reanalysis. Tenure and promotion criteria that explicitly weight replication work, null findings, and methodological rigor shift the career incentives that currently push researchers toward the behaviors that generate false positives. Taken together, these interventions directly target the mechanisms that produce inflated error rates, and there is good reason to think they would substantially reduce the false-positive rate in the published literature. Yet their adoption has been slow, and the reason is not that researchers fail to see their value but that they are individually rational only when adopted collectively. A researcher who unilaterally pre-registers, shares data, and devotes years to replication studies while competitors continue to exploit analytical flexibility simply loses the competition for jobs, grants, and journal space. The transition to better practices is a coordination problem, in which the equilibrium shift requires simultaneous movement by many actors, and such shifts do not occur spontaneously in decentralized systems. The actors with the leverage to force coordination are funding bodies and, secondarily, major journals, because they can make compliance a condition of resources that researchers cannot forgo. Without such enforcement, exhortation to adopt better practices will continue to be absorbed by the existing incentive gradient, and the crisis will persist not because the field does not know how to fix it, but because fixing it requires an institutional actor willing to change the rules of the game.

The replication crisis in psychology underscores a deeper institutional and incentive-structural problem rather than merely a methodological one. The proximate methodological failures, such as underpowered studies, p-hacking, HARKing, and selective outcome reporting, are not primarily due to individual incompetence but are rational adaptations to a publication incentive structure that disproportionately rewards novel, statistically significant findings while marginalizing replication attempts and null results. Researchers operate within a system where career advancement, funding, and professional recognition hinge on frequent publication in high-impact journals, which favor flashy, positive outcomes over rigorous but less glamorous work. This creates a perverse incentive to exploit methodological flexibility to produce publishable results, even at the cost of reliability. The problem is not that researchers are unaware of best practices but that the institutional reward system makes suboptimal methods individually rational, as the costs of rigorous research—such as larger sample sizes or pre-registration—are borne by the individual, while the benefits of questionable practices are immediately rewarded.  

The peer review system, as currently structured, fails to adequately verify methodological soundness because it lacks mechanisms to ensure transparency and reproducibility. Reviewers typically do not have access to raw data, pre-registered hypotheses, or the ability to independently replicate analyses, leaving them unable to detect the subtle but pervasive analytical flexibility that inflates false-positive rates. Moreover, reviewers operate under time constraints and cognitive biases that favor exciting findings over methodological rigor, further entrenching the problem. The system’s reliance on post-hoc scrutiny rather than pre-commitment to methods means that questionable research practices often go undetected, as reviewers cannot feasibly audit every analytical decision. This institutional blind spot allows false positives to proliferate, not because reviewers are negligent, but because the system does not provide them with the tools or incentives to enforce rigor.  

Field-level interventions, such as pre-registration mandates, registered reports, open data requirements, and tenure criteria that value replication, are necessary and sufficient to meaningfully reduce false-positive rates. These reforms align individual incentives with collective epistemic goals by making transparency and reproducibility prerequisites for publication and career advancement. However, their adoption has been slow because they present a collective action problem: no individual researcher or journal can unilaterally impose higher standards without risking competitive disadvantage. Pre-registration, for instance, reduces analytical flexibility but may also decrease a study’s chances of producing publishable results, placing early adopters at a disadvantage. Similarly, journals that prioritize replications may lose submissions to competitors that favor novelty. Thus, systemic change requires coordination—funding bodies, journals, and universities must enforce these standards simultaneously to eliminate free-riding and ensure that the benefits of rigor are universally shared. Without such top-down enforcement, the incentive structure will continue to favor questionable practices, perpetuating the replication crisis.

The replication crisis in psychology reveals a fundamentally institutional and incentive-structural problem because the most visible methodological failures are best understood as predictable responses to the reward system in which researchers work. Underpowered studies, p-hacking, HARKing, and selective outcome reporting are often described as technical or individual failings, but they persist because the professional environment makes them rational. Journals, hiring committees, grant panels, and promotion systems have historically rewarded statistically significant, surprising, and theoretically clean findings far more than careful null results, direct replications, or incremental confirmations. In such an environment, a researcher who runs a small study, explores multiple analytic specifications, reframes an unexpected result as if it had been predicted, or reports only the outcomes that “worked” is responding to incentives that make publishable positive findings the main currency of career advancement. The problem is therefore not simply that individual psychologists lacked methodological sophistication; it is that the system attached professional value to outcomes most likely to emerge from flexible, underpowered, and selectively reported research practices. When novelty and significance are rewarded while replication and null findings are devalued, the production of false positives becomes an institutional pattern rather than a collection of isolated mistakes.

The peer review system, as currently constituted, has not provided sufficient verification of methodological adequacy because it usually evaluates manuscripts rather than research processes. Reviewers typically see a polished narrative, a summary of analyses, and a curated presentation of results, but they often do not have access to raw data, complete analytic histories, pre-specified hypotheses, or evidence that the findings can be independently reproduced. Without mandatory data sharing, pre-registration, or independent replication, peer review cannot reliably distinguish between a genuinely confirmatory test and a result produced through undisclosed flexibility in measurement, exclusion rules, model specification, subgroup analysis, or outcome selection. Reviewers also work under severe time constraints and usually provide unpaid labor alongside their own research and teaching responsibilities, which makes it unrealistic to expect them to reconstruct all possible researcher degrees of freedom from a submitted article. As a result, peer review can assess plausibility, clarity, and surface-level methodological competence, but it is poorly equipped to detect the flexible analytical choices that inflate false-positive rates. The replication crisis therefore exposes not just weak methods, but an institutional verification system that lacks the mechanisms required to check whether reported findings are robust products of pre-specified inquiry.

Field-level interventions are necessary and sufficient to substantially reduce the false-positive rate because the source of the problem lies in collective incentives rather than merely individual intentions. Pre-registration mandates reduce hidden analytic flexibility by requiring hypotheses, outcomes, exclusion rules, and analysis plans to be specified in advance. Registered reports shift the basis of publication from the attractiveness of results to the importance of the question and the rigor of the design, thereby weakening the premium on positive findings. Open data requirements make statistical claims more verifiable and allow errors, questionable analytic choices, and alternative specifications to be examined by others. Tenure and promotion criteria that give real weight to replication work would change the career calculus that currently discourages researchers from investing in studies that confirm, refine, or falsify existing claims. Together, these reforms would substantially reduce the institutional production of false positives by changing what is rewarded, what is visible, and what must be justified before publication. Their adoption is slow because each reform is individually rational only if others adopt it as well: a single researcher who pre-registers, shares data, publishes replications, and accepts null results may be disadvantaged if competitors continue to benefit from more flexible and result-driven practices. This creates a coordination problem that individual researchers cannot solve on their own. Funding-body enforcement is therefore essential, because funders can make transparency, pre-registration, data sharing, and replication incentives conditions of support, thereby aligning individual career incentives with the collective goal of producing reliable psychological science.

The replication crisis in psychology is frequently framed as a failure of individual scientific hygiene, but the proximate methodological errors commonly cited are actually highly rational adaptations to a deeply flawed institutional incentive structure. Practices such as conducting underpowered studies, p-hacking, hypothesizing after the results are known, and selective outcome reporting are not the product of scientific incompetence or ethical deviance. Instead, they represent optimized behaviors designed to survive in an academic ecosystem that disproportionately rewards novel, statistically significant findings while systematically penalizing null results and replication attempts. Because journals prioritize eye-catching, positive discoveries for publication—which in turn dictates hiring, grant funding, and tenure—researchers face an existential mandate to produce clean, positive narratives. In this environment, employing flexible analytical choices to push a p-value below the arbitrary threshold of statistical significance is a logical strategy for professional survival. When the institutional currency is the positive result, the system effectively breeds out rigorous but null-producing methodologies, transforming questionable research practices into standard operating procedures for career advancement.

This incentive-driven distortion is further enabled by a peer review system that, in its current configuration, is structurally incapable of verifying the methodological integrity of submitted work. Peer review operates primarily on trust, lacking the institutional mandates for data sharing, pre-registration of hypotheses, or independent replication that would allow for genuine scrutiny. Because reviewers are typically unpaid, time-constrained volunteers, they are forced to evaluate manuscripts based solely on the highly curated narratives presented by the authors. Under these conditions, it is virtually impossible for reviewers to detect the subtle researcher degrees of freedom—such as undisclosed covariate adjustments, selective dropping of outliers, or post-hoc changes to the dependent variables—that artificially inflate false-positive rates. Without access to the raw data, the analytical code, or a pre-registered protocol, the peer review process serves merely as a filter for narrative coherence rather than a robust check on scientific validity, leaving the underlying methodological manipulations entirely invisible.

To rectify this systemic failure, field-level interventions such as mandatory pre-registration, registered reports, open data requirements, and the explicit weighting of replication studies in tenure and promotion criteria are both necessary and sufficient to drastically reduce the false-positive rate. Registered reports, which secure peer review and acceptance based on methodology before data collection, successfully neutralize the temptation to manipulate data by decoupling publication from the direction of the results. However, the adoption of these structural reforms is painfully slow due to a classic coordination problem. For an individual researcher, unilaterally adopting these rigorous, time-consuming standards is professionally disadvantageous if the rest of the field continues to publish rapid, flashy, and unreplicable findings under the old rules. Consequently, systemic change cannot be achieved through voluntary, bottom-up adoption; it requires top-down enforcement from powerful institutional actors, specifically funding bodies and major university systems, which must mandate these open science practices as non-negotiable conditions for financial support and institutional advancement.

The replication crisis in psychology exposes deep institutional and incentive-driven flaws rather than isolated lapses in individual skill or diligence. Methodological shortcomings such as underpowered studies, p-hacking, HARKing, and selective outcome reporting arise as predictable adaptations by researchers who must navigate a publication system that prizes statistically significant novel findings while offering scant reward or space for replication efforts and null results. Career advancement hinges on producing headline-grabbing positive outcomes in high-impact journals, so investigators rationally allocate resources toward designs that maximize the chance of such outcomes even when those designs lack sufficient statistical power or invite post-hoc adjustments to the data. This pattern persists because the underlying reward structure treats a successful but questionable positive result as more valuable than a rigorously conducted replication or a transparently reported absence of effect.

Peer review in its present form compounds the difficulty by failing to enforce the basic safeguards needed to verify methodological soundness. Journals routinely accept manuscripts without requiring data deposition, pre-registration of hypotheses and analyses, or evidence of prior independent replication, leaving reviewers to evaluate claims on the basis of narrative summaries alone. Operating under severe time pressure and without access to raw data or analysis scripts, reviewers cannot reliably identify the numerous degrees of freedom in data collection, variable coding, and statistical modeling that allow false-positive rates to climb well above nominal levels. Consequently, the gatekeeping process certifies work whose evidential status remains largely unexamined at the level of actual research practice.

Correcting these distortions requires coordinated field-level changes such as mandatory pre-registration, registered reports that commit journals to publication decisions before results are known, open-data policies, and revised tenure standards that assign substantial credit to replication studies. These measures would jointly lower the false-positive rate by aligning publication incentives with transparent and reproducible methods. Yet individual researchers or departments face strong disincentives to adopt them unilaterally, since doing so would place them at a competitive disadvantage relative to peers who continue to operate under the existing regime; only binding requirements imposed by major funding agencies can overcome this collective-action barrier and shift the equilibrium toward higher standards of evidence.

The thesis that causation reduces to regular succession between event-types, inherited from Hume and refined by the deductive-nomological tradition, cannot withstand scrutiny, because the extensional pattern of "whenever C-type events occur, E-type events follow" captures too much and discriminates too little. The classic counterexample is the barometer: a sharp drop in barometric reading is reliably followed by a storm, and the generalization linking the two is as exceptionless as any in ordinary life, yet no one supposes that the needle's descent causes the atmospheric disturbance. The regularity is real but derivative, grounded in a common cause—the fall in ambient air pressure—that produces both the instrument's behavior and the meteorological event. Analogous cases proliferate: day regularly succeeds night, the reading on one synchronized clock regularly precedes the chime of another, and symptoms of a disease regularly accompany one another without any one symptom causing the rest. In each instance, a regularity theorist is forced either to count the correlation as causal, which violates our firmest judgments, or to append auxiliary conditions—temporal priority, spatiotemporal contiguity, nomological subsumption—that either fail to exclude the problem cases or smuggle in causal notions the analysis was meant to reduce. The deeper diagnosis is that mere co-occurrence, however lawlike, is a symmetric and undirected relation among event-types, while causation is asymmetric and directed; no amount of refinement internal to the regularity framework supplies the missing directionality.

The interventionist account developed by James Woodward supplies precisely what the regularity account lacks by analyzing causation in terms of what would happen under hypothetical manipulations of the putative cause. On Woodward's view, C is a cause of E, relative to a background of variables, just in case there is some possible intervention on C—an exogenous surgical change that sets the value of C independently of its usual determinants and alters nothing else except via C—under which the value of E would correspondingly change, and the dependency between C and E remains invariant across some suitable range of such interventions. Applied to the barometer, the account yields the correct verdict immediately: were we to intervene directly on the needle, forcing it downward by mechanical means while holding atmospheric pressure fixed, no storm would ensue; the correlation between reading and weather does not survive an intervention on the reading itself, so the reading does not cause the weather. By contrast, an intervention on atmospheric pressure does change both the needle and the storm, correctly identifying pressure as the common cause. The interventionist framework thus recovers the asymmetry of causation from the asymmetry of manipulability: effects do not propagate backward along causal arrows, so wiggling an effect leaves its causes untouched, while wiggling a cause disturbs its effects. Causal relations emerge as those counterfactual dependencies that are robust under the specific class of counterfactuals corresponding to ideal interventions, a class far more restrictive and better behaved than the generic counterfactuals that caused trouble for earlier similarity-based analyses.

The interventionist account further illuminates why randomized controlled experiments enjoy their distinctive epistemic authority in the sciences, since the design of such trials is a concrete attempt to realize, within the constraints of actual practice, the ideal interventions the theory invokes. When investigators randomize subjects to treatment and control arms, they sever the putative cause from the ordinary web of antecedents—genetic predispositions, socioeconomic circumstances, prior health behaviors, self-selection—that would otherwise be correlated with it and would otherwise confound inference from observed regularities to causal structure. The assignment of treatment is made to depend on a chance device rather than on any variable that could independently influence the outcome, which is just what Woodward's definition of an intervention requires: the cause is set exogenously, through a process that bears no relation to the outcome except through the cause itself. Any difference in outcomes between the arms must then reflect a dependency that would survive manipulation of the cause, and that is precisely the dependency the interventionist identifies with causation. Observational studies, however rich in regularities they display, cannot discharge this requirement, because the putative cause there retains its ordinary antecedents, leaving open whether the observed correlation reflects a genuine cause-to-effect dependency or merely a shared ancestry with some lurking variable. The experimental intervention cuts those ancestral links by fiat, which is why a well-designed randomized trial can settle in one stroke causal questions that unlimited observational data cannot. That the interventionist account predicts and explains this methodological fact, rather than treating it as a brute piece of scientific folklore, counts as substantial evidence in its favor and against any analysis content with mere regular succession.

The thesis that causation cannot be adequately analyzed as mere regular succession between types of events is well-supported by examining the limitations of regularity accounts and the strengths of interventionist alternatives. Regularity accounts, which reduce causation to the observation of constant conjunctions between events, fail to distinguish genuine causal relations from accidental or common-cause correlations. For instance, a falling barometer reading is regularly followed by a storm, yet the barometer does not cause the storm. Instead, both events are effects of a common cause—a drop in atmospheric pressure. This example illustrates that regularity alone cannot capture the asymmetry inherent in causal relationships, as it conflates causation with mere correlation. Without a mechanism to differentiate between causal and non-causal regularities, regularity accounts provide an incomplete and often misleading analysis of causation.

In contrast, interventionist accounts, developed by James Woodward, address this deficiency by identifying causal relations with dependencies that remain invariant under ideal interventions on the putative cause. According to this view, a causal relationship exists if manipulating the cause in an ideal way—holding all other factors constant—leads to a change in the effect. This approach successfully distinguishes genuine causation from spurious correlations by focusing on the behavior of the system under controlled manipulations. For example, intervening to artificially lower the barometer reading would not produce a storm, confirming that the barometer does not cause the storm. By incorporating the concept of intervention, this account captures the asymmetry and directionality of causation that regularity accounts overlook, providing a more robust framework for analyzing causal relationships.

Moreover, the interventionist account explains the epistemic privilege of randomized controlled experiments, which are widely regarded as the gold standard for establishing causal claims. Randomized controlled experiments approximate ideal interventions by severing the putative cause from its ordinary antecedents, thereby isolating its effect on the outcome. Randomization ensures that any observed correlation between the cause and effect is not confounded by hidden variables or common causes. This methodological design aligns with the interventionist principle that causal relationships are those that remain invariant under manipulation. Thus, the interventionist account not only provides a theoretical foundation for understanding causation but also justifies the practical superiority of experimental methods in uncovering causal truths. By integrating these insights, the interventionist framework offers a compelling alternative to the inadequacies of regularity-based analyses.

Causation cannot be adequately analyzed as mere regular succession between types of events because regularity is too indiscriminate. If one event type is regularly followed by another, that fact alone does not show that the first produces, generates, or makes a difference to the second. A falling barometer reading is regularly followed by a storm, but the falling reading does not cause the storm. Rather, both are effects of a common atmospheric condition: changes in air pressure. The regular sequence is real, but it is not causal in the relevant direction. This shows that a regularity account mistakes reliable association for causal connection. It lacks the resources to distinguish cases in which one event genuinely brings about another from cases in which the two are merely correlated because of a shared background cause or accidental pattern.

Interventionist accounts, especially as developed by James Woodward, succeed at precisely this point by analyzing causation in terms of stable dependence under ideal interventions. On this view, the crucial question is not whether events of one type are regularly followed by events of another type, but whether changing the putative cause by an appropriate intervention would change the effect. A causal relation exists when the effect depends on the cause in a way that remains invariant under interventions that alter the cause while holding fixed other relevant influences. If one could intervene to change the barometer reading alone, without changing the atmospheric conditions, the storm would not thereby be changed. By contrast, if one intervenes on a genuine cause, the effect varies accordingly. The interventionist account therefore captures the difference-making structure that regular succession by itself misses.

This also explains the epistemic privilege of randomized controlled experiments. Such experiments are powerful because their design approximates an ideal intervention on the putative cause. Random assignment severs the treatment or exposure from its ordinary antecedents, preventing preexisting differences among subjects from determining who receives the intervention. As a result, correlations between the assigned treatment and the outcome are not merely ordinary regularities embedded in a web of background causes; they are evidence of what happens when the putative cause is manipulated independently. The randomized controlled experiment is therefore especially well suited to reveal causal relations because it creates conditions under which the relevant dependency can be observed apart from the confounding patterns that make regular succession insufficient.

The reduction of causation to mere regular succession, a tradition tracing back to David Hume, fails to capture the true nature of causal relations because it cannot distinguish between genuine causal connections and mere correlation. According to regularity theories, for one event type to cause another is simply for events of the first type to be regularly followed by events of the second type. However, this definition is far too permissive, as it mistakenly classifies non-causal, regularly occurring sequences as causal. A classic illustration of this failure is the relationship between a falling barometer reading and the onset of a storm. Because a drop in the barometer is regularly followed by a storm, a pure regularity account must conclude that the falling barometer causes the storm. In reality, both events are joint effects of a common cause, namely, a drop in atmospheric pressure. Because the regularity account lacks any conceptual machinery to distinguish between a direct causal path and a correlation produced by a shared antecedent, it remains fundamentally inadequate as an analysis of causation.

This profound limitation is overcome by the interventionist account of causation, most prominently developed by James Woodward, which replaces passive observation of regularities with the active concept of manipulation. Under Woodward's framework, a variable X causes a variable Y if and only if the value of Y would change under an ideal intervention on X. An ideal intervention is a hypothetical or actual manipulation that changes the value of X in such a way that X's value is determined entirely by the intervention itself, thereby severing X from its usual causal antecedents, while ensuring that the intervention has no direct influence on Y through any pathway other than X. This account successfully resolves the barometer puzzle: if an experimenter were to intervene and manually force the barometer needle down, the storm would not occur, showing that the correlation does not remain invariant under intervention. Conversely, if one were to intervene on the atmospheric pressure itself, the storm would still occur. By identifying causal relationships with those dependencies that remain invariant under such ideal interventions, the interventionist account successfully distinguishes genuine causal relationships from accidental or common-cause correlations.

Furthermore, the interventionist framework provides a powerful explanation for the unique epistemic privilege accorded to randomized controlled trials in the natural and social sciences. The very design of a randomized controlled trial is intended to physically approximate the philosophical ideal of an intervention by randomly assigning the putative cause, such as a medical treatment, to subjects. This process of randomization effectively severs the putative cause from its ordinary, confounding antecedents, such as genetics, lifestyle, or socioeconomic status, which might otherwise produce a misleading correlation with the outcome. By ensuring that the treatment variable is dictated solely by a random mechanism, researchers simulate an ideal intervention, guaranteeing that any remaining correlation between the treatment and the outcome must be causal rather than spurious. The interventionist account thus illuminates why randomized controlled trials are uniquely capable of yielding causal knowledge, grounding their scientific authority in their ability to isolate invariant relationships through the deliberate disruption of natural regularities.

Causation cannot be adequately analyzed as mere regular succession between types of events, for regularity accounts fail to distinguish genuine causal relations from accidental or common-cause correlations, since a falling barometer reading is regularly followed by a storm without causing it. Such accounts therefore leave open the possibility that any observed regularity might be spurious in precisely this way, offering no resources for isolating those patterns that reflect genuine production or influence rather than mere coincidence or shared antecedents. 
Interventionist accounts developed by Woodward succeed where regularity accounts fail by identifying causal relations with dependencies that remain invariant under ideal interventions on the putative cause. On this view a variable X counts as a cause of Y precisely when there exists a possible intervention on X that would change the value of Y while holding fixed all other relevant variables, thereby capturing a stable relationship that persists across a range of manipulations rather than one that merely happens to obtain in the actual course of events. 
The interventionist account explains the epistemic privilege of randomized controlled experiments, whose design approximates an ideal intervention by severing the putative cause from its ordinary antecedents. By assigning subjects to treatment or control conditions through a random mechanism, such trials break the usual connections between the intervention variable and its background causes, thereby isolating the dependence of the outcome on the treatment alone and furnishing evidence that would be unavailable from passive observation of regularities.

The concept of biological function occupies a central place in the life sciences, and how we analyze it determines whether functional discourse can bear the explanatory and normative weight biologists routinely place upon it. Two broad traditions have competed to provide this analysis: the etiological or selected-effect tradition, which locates function in a trait's selection history, and the causal-role tradition descending from Cummins, which identifies function with any contribution a trait makes to a containing system's capacities. There are compelling reasons to prefer the etiological approach, since it alone secures the normativity, objectivity, and explanatory force that functional attributions appear to possess.

The first consideration concerns normativity. Functional ascriptions in biology are not merely descriptive; they license claims about what a trait is supposed to do, and consequently about when it fails to do what it should. A diseased heart that cannot pump blood still has the function of pumping blood, and a cone cell in a colorblind retina still has the function of discriminating wavelengths even when it cannot. This normative dimension, including the very possibility of malfunction, is captured naturally by the selected-effect account. If a trait's function is the effect for which its ancestors were selected, then a token of that trait has a function it may fail to perform, since what it is for is fixed by evolutionary history rather than by its current dispositions. A purely dispositional analysis, by contrast, cannot generate this gap between what a trait does and what it ought to do. If function were simply a matter of what a trait is disposed to produce, then a trait that lacks the disposition would lack the function, and malfunction would become conceptually impossible: a non-pumping heart would simply fail to have the pumping function at all, rather than failing to perform its function. Since biologists plainly treat malfunction as a coherent and important category, only an account that distinguishes function from current disposition can accommodate biological practice, and the etiological account does so by anchoring function in ancestral selection rather than present capacity.

The second consideration concerns objectivity. Cummins-style causal-role analyses define function in terms of a trait's contribution to some capacity of a containing system, where that capacity is itself picked out by the explanatory project of an inquirer. The difficulty is that any trait makes countless contributions to countless systemic capacities, many of which are intuitively accidental rather than functional. The heart contributes to blood circulation, but it also contributes to the production of rhythmic thumping sounds useful to physicians with stethoscopes, to the weight distribution of the thorax, and to a host of other systemic outcomes. To isolate circulation as the heart's function rather than, say, sound production, the causal-role theorist must appeal to which capacity the investigator has chosen to analyze. Function thereby becomes relative to explanatory interests, and the distinction between genuine functions and merely accidental effects collapses into a distinction between effects we happen to care about and effects we do not. This surrenders the objectivity of functional attribution: whether the heart's function is to circulate blood would depend not on the heart itself but on what question an inquirer happens to be asking. The etiological account avoids this consequence because selection history is a mind-independent matter of fact. The heart was selected for pumping blood and not for producing sounds, regardless of what any investigator finds interesting, and this historical fact fixes its function objectively.

The third consideration concerns explanatory force. When a biologist says that the function of a trait is such-and-such, this claim is typically taken to explain something about the trait, in particular why organisms of the relevant kind have it. The etiological account vindicates this explanatory pretension directly. To cite the selected effect of a trait is to answer the question of why the trait is present in the population: it is present because ancestral variants that produced that effect were differentially retained by natural selection. Functional claims thus do genuine explanatory work, situating the trait within a historical process that accounts for its existence and distribution. Causal-role analyses, by contrast, can only describe what a trait currently contributes to a system; they cannot explain why the trait is there to make the contribution in the first place. Saying that the heart contributes to circulation tells us something about how the organism currently operates, but it leaves wholly untouched the question of why organisms are built with hearts at all. Only by appealing to selection history does functional discourse acquire the retrospective, explanatory dimension that distinguishes it from mere systemic description, and only the etiological account makes this dimension constitutive of what functions are.

The analysis of biological function is best approached through an etiological lens, specifically the selected-effect account, rather than a purely causal-role framework, as the former provides a more robust and comprehensive understanding of function. Selected-effect accounts define a trait’s function as the effect for which its ancestors were naturally selected, and this approach uniquely explains the normativity inherent in functional attributions. Unlike causal-role accounts, which treat function as a mere dispositional property, selected-effect accounts accommodate the possibility of malfunction. For instance, a heart’s function is to pump blood because this effect conferred a selective advantage on ancestors with hearts. However, a heart that fails to pump blood is malfunctioning, even if it still produces other effects, such as rhythmic sounds. This normative dimension—the distinction between proper function and malfunction—cannot be captured by purely dispositional analyses, which reduce function to whatever a trait happens to do in a given system. Thus, selected-effect accounts provide a principled basis for understanding functional norms, a critical feature of biological explanation.

Causal-role accounts, as articulated by Robert Cummins, identify a trait’s function with its causal contribution to a broader system’s capacities. While this approach offers a pragmatic framework for analyzing complex systems, it fails to distinguish a trait’s function from its accidental effects without appealing to the explanatory interests of the investigator. For example, the heart’s rhythmic sounds contribute to systemic capacities, such as providing auditory cues for medical diagnosis, but these sounds are not its function. Without invoking selective history, causal-role accounts must relativize function to the goals or interests of the observer, thereby surrendering the objectivity of functional attribution. In contrast, selected-effect accounts ground functional claims in the objective, historical facts of natural selection, avoiding the subjectivity inherent in causal-role analyses. This objectivity is crucial for scientific explanations, which seek to uncover facts about the natural world rather than reflect the investigator’s perspective.

Moreover, etiological accounts alone vindicate the explanatory force of functional claims by addressing the historical question of why a trait is present. When we assert that the function of the heart is to pump blood, we are not merely describing a current disposition but explaining the evolutionary pressures that led to the heart’s existence and persistence. Causal-role accounts, by contrast, are limited to describing what a trait does within a system, offering no insight into its origins or maintenance over evolutionary time. This historical dimension is essential for understanding biological traits, as it connects their current properties to the selective processes that shaped them. By citing a trait’s selected effect, etiological accounts provide a deeper and more satisfying explanation of biological phenomena, one that goes beyond surface-level descriptions to uncover the underlying reasons for a trait’s presence and design. Thus, the etiological approach is indispensable for a complete and objective analysis of biological function.

Biological function is best understood etiologically because functions are normative: a trait can perform its function well or badly, and it can have a function even when it fails to perform it. Selected-effect accounts explain this by identifying a trait’s function with the effect for which earlier instances of that trait were selected. The function of the heart is to pump blood because ancestral hearts contributed to survival and reproduction by pumping blood, and that effect explains why hearts of that kind were preserved and reproduced in the lineage. This makes sense of malfunction. A diseased heart that fails to pump blood properly still has pumping blood as its function, because its function is fixed by the selection history of hearts, not by its present causal powers. By contrast, a purely dispositional analysis identifies function with what a trait is disposed to do, or with what it in fact does under certain conditions. Such an account cannot adequately distinguish functioning from malfunctioning. If a heart is disposed only to fibrillate, or if an eye is incapable of seeing, a purely dispositional account has difficulty explaining why these are defective instances rather than traits with different functions. Etiology supplies the missing standard: the trait is evaluated against the effect that explains its historical retention.

Causal-role accounts in the tradition of Cummins analyze function in terms of the contribution a component makes to the capacities of a containing system. On this view, the function of a trait is whatever causal role it plays in some larger explanatory analysis. But biological traits have many causal effects, and not all of them are functions. The heart pumps blood, makes sounds, adds weight to the body, consumes energy, and can obstruct a surgeon’s access to other organs. A causal-role analysis can call any of these a function if the chosen explanatory project makes that effect relevant. This means that the line between a function and an accidental effect depends on the investigator’s explanatory interests. If one is explaining circulation, pumping blood is selected; if one is explaining diagnostic auscultation, producing sounds is selected; if one is explaining body mass, contributing weight is selected. The attribution becomes relative to a chosen analysis rather than fixed by the biological history of the trait. Etiological accounts preserve objectivity by distinguishing the effect that explains the trait’s existence from the many effects the trait happens to have. The function is not whatever an investigator finds useful to cite, but the effect for which the trait was selected.

Etiological accounts also best explain why functional claims have distinctive explanatory force. To say that the function of the heart is to pump blood is not merely to describe a current activity of the heart. It is to answer why organisms have hearts of that type at all. The selected effect explains the presence and persistence of the trait in the lineage: hearts are there because ancestral hearts pumped blood in ways that contributed to reproductive success. This historical explanation is what gives functional language its biological depth. A purely causal-role statement says what a trait does within a system now; it locates the trait in an organized causal economy. But it does not by itself explain why that trait exists rather than not, or why organisms came to possess it. Etiological function does. It connects current organization to evolutionary history, showing how a trait’s present role is grounded in past selection. For that reason, functional claims in biology are most fully explanatory when they are etiological: they identify not merely an effect of the trait, but the effect that accounts for the trait’s being there.

The etiological framework, specifically the selected-effect account, provides the only adequate foundation for biological function because it successfully accounts for the inherent normativity of functional language, including the crucial concept of malfunction. According to the selected-effect view, the function of a biological trait is defined by the specific effect for which that trait was favored by natural selection in ancestral organisms. This historical grounding establishes an objective normative standard of what the trait is supposed to do, regardless of its current physical state or performance. By tying function to evolutionary history, the etiological account explains how a trait can fail to perform its function. For instance, a malformed or diseased heart that is incapable of pumping blood still possesses the function of pumping blood, because it is a member of a trait-kind that was selected for that specific effect. A purely dispositional or causal-role analysis, which defines function solely in terms of current causal contributions, cannot accommodate this distinction. If function is merely a current disposition, then a heart that cannot pump blood simply lacks the disposition to do so, meaning its failure to pump cannot be classified as a malfunction; it is merely behaving according to its current physical state. Thus, only the etiological account preserves the normative distinction between what a trait actually does and what it is biologically supposed to do.

Furthermore, causal-role accounts, such as those modeled after Robert Cummins, are fundamentally incapable of distinguishing a trait’s genuine biological functions from its mere accidental effects without surrendering the objectivity of functional attribution. In a Cummins-style analysis, a function is identified as any causal contribution a component makes to a larger capacity of a containing system. Without the historical constraint of natural selection, however, there is no principled, mind-independent way to separate a trait's evolutionary purpose from its coincidental side effects. For example, the heart contributes to the capacity of the body to circulate blood, but it also contributes to the capacity of medical professionals to hear heartbeats through a stethoscope. Under a purely causal-role view, both of these contributions count as functions unless one artificially privileges certain system capacities over others. To make this distinction, causal-role theorists must relativize functional attributions to the specific explanatory interests of the investigator. Consequently, whether a trait has a function, and what that function is, becomes a subjective matter dependent on the cognitive goals of the scientist rather than an objective, mind-independent fact about the organism itself. The etiological account avoids this relativism by grounding functions in the objective, historical process of natural selection, ensuring that functional claims remain discoveries about nature rather than inventions of the observer.

Finally, etiological accounts alone vindicate the unique explanatory force of functional claims in biological science by answering the fundamental question of why a trait is present in an organism. When biologists assert that the function of the kidney is to filter blood, they are not merely offering a mechanical description of what the kidney currently does; they are providing a teleological explanation for why kidneys exist in the organismal population. The etiological account directly addresses this historical question by showing that the current presence of the trait is a causal consequence of past selection for that very effect; kidneys exist today because ancestral kidneys filtered blood, thereby enhancing the fitness of those ancestors. In contrast, causal-role accounts are restricted to describing the current, synchronic operations of a system, answering the question of how a mechanism currently operates rather than why it exists. Citing a trait's current causal role cannot explain why the organism possesses that trait in the first place, as a current effect cannot causally explain its own pre-existing structural cause. By linking function to the selective history that brought the trait into being, the etiological account provides a robustly explanatory framework that justifies why functional language is indispensable to evolutionary biology.

Biological function in living organisms is best understood through an etiological lens that traces back to the selective history of traits rather than through a purely causal-role analysis that focuses solely on current contributions to system capacities. Selected-effect accounts identify a trait's function with the effect for which its ancestors were selected, and this framework explains the normativity of function, including the possibility of malfunction, which a purely dispositional analysis cannot accommodate because it merely describes what a trait is capable of doing without reference to any standard of proper performance that could be violated. 

Causal-role accounts following Cummins face difficulties in distinguishing a trait's function from its accidental effects, as they must ultimately relativize function to the explanatory interests of the investigator, thereby surrendering the objectivity of functional attribution and making functions dependent on subjective choices rather than inherent features of biological systems. 

Etiological accounts alone vindicate the explanatory force of functional claims, since citing a trait's selected effect answers the historical question of why the trait is present rather than merely describing what it currently does, thereby grounding functional explanations in evolutionary history in a manner that causal-role accounts inherently lack.

Knowledge gained through testimony constitutes an irreducible epistemic category, one that cannot be analyzed away into the hearer's own perceptions, memories, and inductive generalizations about the reliability of speakers. The reductionist program, descending from Hume, holds that a hearer is justified in accepting what she is told only insofar as she possesses independent evidence, drawn from her own experience, that testimony of the relevant kind tends to be true. Against this program, three considerations converge to show that testimonial knowledge rests on foundations the hearer cannot herself supply.

The first consideration, pressed with particular force by C. A. J. Coady, concerns the sheer scale of our testimonial dependence. The ordinary adult believes, on the word of others, a staggering range of propositions: that there is a country called Peru, that Napoleon lost at Waterloo, that water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen, that the heart pumps blood, that there are cities she has never visited and historical events she did not witness. For reductionism to succeed, the believer would need to have built up, from her own direct checks, an inductive base sufficient to warrant confidence in the various kinds of testimony she accepts. But no human being is in a position to carry out such verification for more than a vanishing fraction of her sources. One cannot personally confirm the honesty of textbook authors, journalists, cartographers, physicians, teachers, and the countless informants whose words shape one's picture of the world. The reductionist's inductive base, when honestly surveyed, turns out to be minuscule relative to the testimonial edifice it is supposed to support. The project of grounding testimonial belief in the hearer's own prior checks is therefore not merely difficult but structurally unavailable; the resources demanded by reductionism simply do not exist in the cognitive life of any actual knower.

The second consideration concerns the epistemic situation of young children. Children acquire enormous bodies of information through testimony long before they possess the sophisticated inferential machinery that reductionism requires. A three-year-old who learns that lions live in Africa, that her grandmother's name is Margaret, that stoves can burn, or that the round object in the sky is called the moon has not conducted, and could not conduct, an inductive survey of adult reliability across domains. She lacks the conceptual apparatus to formulate hypotheses about the correlation between utterance and truth, lacks the memory stores to accumulate the relevant evidence, and lacks the logical skills to draw general conclusions from particular cases. Yet it would be absurd to deny that children come to know a great deal through what they are told. If reductionism were correct, such early learning would not count as knowledge at all, and the entire developmental trajectory by which humans enter the community of knowers would be epistemically illegitimate at its root. Since children plainly do acquire genuine knowledge through testimony, the justification of such knowledge cannot consist in inferences the child is incapable of making.

The third consideration, developed by John Hardwig in his analyses of epistemic dependence, concerns the structure of modern scientific knowledge itself. Contemporary research is organized through an elaborate division of cognitive labor: experiments in high-energy physics involve hundreds of collaborators, each responsible for a specialized component of the apparatus or analysis; medical studies rely on statisticians, clinicians, and laboratory technicians whose work no single investigator can fully reproduce; published papers in nearly every field cite results that the citing author has not personally verified and often could not verify without years of additional training. The physicist who signs a paper on a particle detection relies on the testimony of colleagues who built the detector, calibrated the instruments, wrote the analysis code, and interpreted the raw data. If reductionism were correct, the physicist's belief in the reported result would be unjustified unless she had independently checked these contributions, which she has not and in most cases could not. Yet the scientific community manifestly produces knowledge, and the individual researcher who affirms a collaborative result does so with epistemic warrant. The warrant must therefore come, at least in part, from trust in the testimony of colleagues, trust that cannot be cashed out in the individual's own perceptions and inferences. Scientific knowledge, the paradigm of rigorous epistemic achievement, is thus itself constituted in part by irreducible testimonial dependence.

Taken together, these three considerations show that testimony is a genuine and independent source of knowledge. The scope of ordinary belief outruns any inductive base a single mind could assemble; the testimonial learning of children precedes the inferential capacities reductionism presupposes; and the collaborative character of science makes even its most refined products rest on trust in the words of others. Testimonial knowledge is not perception, memory, or inference in disguise, but a distinct epistemic kind, woven into the very fabric of human cognitive life.

The thesis that knowledge acquired through testimony cannot be reduced to knowledge grounded in the hearer’s own perception, memory, and inductive inference is compellingly supported by three key considerations. First, as Coady has argued, the sheer scale of testimonial knowledge on which individuals rely makes reductionism practically untenable. In ordinary life, people depend on a vast network of sources—teachers, journalists, scientists, historians, and others—for information about the world. No individual has the capacity to independently verify the track record of more than a small fraction of these sources. For example, a person cannot personally observe historical events, conduct every scientific experiment, or verify every news report they encounter. Attempting to reduce testimonial knowledge to perception, memory, and inductive inference would require an impractical and unsustainable level of epistemic labor. This reliance on testimony is not a failure of epistemic rigor but a necessary feature of human cognition, given the limits of individual experience and the complexity of the world. Reductionism, therefore, fails to account for the practical realities of how knowledge is acquired and sustained in everyday life.

Second, the developmental trajectory of knowledge acquisition in young children underscores the irreducible nature of testimonial knowledge. Children absorb vast amounts of information through testimony long before they develop the inferential capacities required by reductionist accounts. For instance, a child learns language, basic facts about the world, and social norms primarily through the testimony of parents, caregivers, and teachers. At this early stage, children lack the ability to critically evaluate the reliability of their sources or to independently verify the truth of what they are told. Yet, this knowledge forms the foundation for their future understanding and reasoning. Reductionism, which insists that testimonial knowledge must be justified through the hearer’s own perception, memory, and inference, cannot explain how young children acquire knowledge so effectively and pervasively through testimony. This suggests that testimonial knowledge operates as a distinct and fundamental epistemic source, irreducible to other cognitive processes.

Third, the division of cognitive labor in contemporary science, as analyzed by Hardwig, demonstrates the irreducibly testimonial nature of scientific knowledge itself. Scientific research is highly specialized, with individual scientists relying on the findings of colleagues whose work they cannot personally replicate or verify. For example, a physicist may depend on the results of complex experiments conducted by a team in another country, or a biologist may build on data generated by colleagues using advanced technologies. This epistemic interdependence is not a flaw but a strength of the scientific enterprise, enabling the accumulation of knowledge that no single individual could achieve alone. Reductionism, which seeks to ground testimonial knowledge in the hearer’s own perceptual and inferential capacities, cannot account for this reliance on the testimony of others. Scientific knowledge, therefore, rests on an irreducible foundation of trust in the testimony of fellow researchers, highlighting the indispensable role of testimony in epistemic practices even at the highest levels of inquiry. Together, these three claims—rooted in the practical limits of individual verification, the cognitive development of children, and the collaborative nature of science—provide a robust defense of the thesis that testimonial knowledge cannot be reduced to perception, memory, and inductive inference.

Knowledge acquired through testimony cannot be reduced to knowledge grounded solely in the hearer’s own perception, memory, and inductive inference, because ordinary epistemic life depends on a range of sources whose reliability no individual could independently establish. As Coady argued, the reductionist picture asks too much: it requires the hearer to justify reliance on testimony by appealing to observed correlations between what people say and how things turn out, but no person is in a position to check more than a tiny fraction of the reports on which ordinary belief depends. Much of what one knows about history, geography, medicine, law, distant events, institutions, and other people’s lives comes from chains of testimony that extend far beyond one’s personal experience. One may confirm some reports, but those confirmations are themselves usually dependent on further testimony: maps, records, measurements, expert statements, archives, and educational materials. The hearer’s own perception and memory provide only a narrow basis compared with the vast body of beliefs acquired from others. Since ordinary knowledge depends on sources whose general track record cannot be independently surveyed by each individual, testimonial knowledge cannot in practice be reconstructed as the outcome of private inductive verification.

The irreducibility of testimony is even clearer in the case of young children. Children acquire enormous bodies of knowledge from parents, teachers, caregivers, and other speakers before they possess the cognitive resources needed to justify testimony in the reductionist manner. They learn the names of objects, the identities of people, the meanings of words, the existence of places they have never seen, rules of conduct, basic facts about animals, bodies, numbers, and social life, and countless claims about the past and the future. This learning does not wait upon an independently established inductive theory of speaker reliability. A young child cannot first collect a large sample of testimonial successes and failures, assess the competence and sincerity of informants, and then infer that testimony is generally trustworthy. Testimony is instead one of the primary routes by which the child comes to possess the concepts, categories, and background beliefs that later make sophisticated inference possible. If testimonial justification required prior reduction to the child’s own perceptual and inductive base, then much of early knowledge would be inexplicable. The developmental order is the reverse: children come to know through testimony before they are capable of the kind of independent epistemic checking that reductionism demands.

The same point holds at the most advanced levels of inquiry, especially in contemporary science. As Hardwig emphasized, modern scientific knowledge is produced through a division of cognitive labor in which researchers depend on the testimony of other researchers whose work they cannot personally verify in full. A scientist may rely on data generated by technicians, statistical analyses performed by collaborators, instruments calibrated by specialists, background theories established in other fields, and experimental results reported in journals by teams with highly specialized expertise. No individual researcher can personally repeat all the experiments, inspect all the equipment, master all the relevant subdisciplines, or audit every calculation on which a scientific conclusion depends. Scientific knowledge is therefore not simply the possession of isolated individuals who have grounded every belief in their own observation and inference. It is sustained by networks of trust, credentials, disciplinary norms, and expert dependence. The cognitive achievements of science arise precisely because researchers accept and build upon the testimony of others in circumstances where personal verification is not available. Thus even paradigmatic knowledge in the sciences rests irreducibly on testimonial trust rather than on the hearer’s independent perceptual, memorial, and inductive resources alone.

The epistemic status of testimony is fundamental to our understanding of human knowledge, as the vast majority of what we claim to know is received from the assertions of others rather than discovered through our own direct experience. The philosophical position of reductionism attempts to devalue testimony by asserting that testimonial knowledge must be justified through, and thus reduced to, the hearer’s own non-testimonial faculties of perception, memory, and inductive inference. However, this reductionist project fails because testimony constitutes an autonomous, irreducible source of justification. To demand that testimonial justification rest entirely on individual empirical verification is to ignore the inescapable social reality of our epistemic lives, the developmental trajectory of human cognition, and the collaborative structure of advanced scientific inquiry.

The practical impossibility of the reductionist project is powerfully demonstrated by C.A.J. Coady’s critique of the requirement that hearers must possess an empirically verified track record of a speaker's reliability before accepting their testimony. Coady argues that no single individual is in a position to independently verify the track record of more than a tiny fraction of the sources upon which their ordinary beliefs depend. To establish the reliability of a witness or an authority without relying on testimony itself would require an individual to personally observe the facts in question, correlate them with the speaker’s assertions, and build a statistically significant database of accuracy. In reality, our reliance on maps, historical documents, news reports, and consumer labels is so pervasive that any attempt to personally verify these sources using only our own senses and memory would immediately collapse. Because we must rely on other testimonies to verify any single testimony, the database of pure, non-testimonial observations we possess is far too impoverished to justify our vast web of beliefs. Consequently, a reductionist justification of testimony is utterly unavailable in practice, leaving us with the choice of either embracing radical skepticism or recognizing testimony as an independent epistemic source.

This irreducibility is further confirmed by observing how human beings first acquire knowledge, particularly during early childhood. Young children acquire vast bodies of knowledge through the testimony of parents, teachers, and caregivers long before they possess the sophisticated inferential resources that reductionism requires for testimonial justification. Before a child can perform the complex inductive reasoning necessary to evaluate a speaker’s reliability, detect biases, or calculate the probability of a claim’s truth, they must first acquire a language and a foundational framework of facts about the world. This foundational knowledge, such as the names of objects, the dangers of certain behaviors, and basic geographical facts, is accepted on trust. If children were required to possess independent, non-testimonial reasons to justify their trust in their parents' words, they could never begin the process of learning. The reductionist account cannot explain this primary acquisition of knowledge, as it mistakenly presupposes that the capacity for critical inductive evaluation precedes the acquisition of testimonial belief, whereas the developmental reality is precisely the reverse.

The necessity of irreducible testimonial trust is not merely a feature of childhood development or everyday practical limitations; it also characterizes the very pinnacle of human intellectual achievement in contemporary science. As John Hardwig has analyzed, the modern division of cognitive labor means that scientific progress relies on highly collaborative research wherein no single scientist can personally verify every component of a project. In fields ranging from high-energy physics to complex medical trials, papers are frequently co-authored by dozens of specialists, each contributing data, mathematical models, or experimental results that require highly specific expertise to produce and interpret. A single researcher cannot possess the time, the specialized training, or the physical resources to independently check the work of all their collaborators. Consequently, scientific knowledge itself rests irreducibly on testimonial trust among researchers. If scientists refused to trust the testimony of their colleagues without independent verification, scientific progress would grind to a halt. The very structure of contemporary science thus demonstrates that our most rigorous and reliable knowledge is fundamentally social and cannot be reduced to the individualistic epistemic resources of perception, memory, and induction.

The thesis that knowledge acquired through testimony cannot be reduced to knowledge grounded in the hearer's own perception, memory, and inductive inference finds support in the practical limits that confront any attempt to ground testimony solely in those resources. As Coady argued, no individual is in a position to verify independently the track record of more than a small fraction of the sources on whom ordinary belief depends, so a reductionist justification of testimony is unavailable in practice. The sheer number and variety of informants whose reports shape everyday knowledge exceed what any single person could check through direct observation and inference, leaving reductionism without the empirical foundation it requires.

Young children acquire vast bodies of knowledge through testimony before they possess the inferential resources that reductionism requires for testimonial justification. They absorb information about language, objects, social norms, and countless other domains from caregivers and others at an age when they lack the conceptual sophistication needed to assess track records or perform the inductive calculations that a reductionist account demands. This developmental sequence indicates that testimonial knowledge functions prior to and independently of the perceptual and inferential apparatus to which reductionism would tie it.

The division of cognitive labor in contemporary science, analyzed by Hardwig, makes researchers epistemically dependent on colleagues whose results they cannot personally check, so that scientific knowledge itself rests irreducibly on testimonial trust. Specialists routinely rely on experimental findings, data sets, and theoretical derivations produced by others whose methods and competence they cannot replicate or audit through their own perception and inference alone. Such dependence shows that even the most rigorous forms of empirical knowledge incorporate an element of testimony that resists reduction to individual perceptual and inductive grounds.

Idealized scientific models trade literal accuracy for something more valuable: they expose the structural features of nature that actually do explanatory work. A frictionless plane, an infinite breeding population, a point mass concentrating finite matter at a dimensionless location—each is strictly false of any real system, yet each enables us to see what makes the phenomenon in question the kind of phenomenon it is. The role of such idealizations is not to approximate reality more and more finely, as if the goal were a scale model, but to perform a kind of controlled subtraction. By setting friction to zero, the Galilean analysis of inclined motion isolates the gravitational component that makes bodies accelerate down slopes; by treating a population as infinite, population genetics isolates the selective and mutational pressures whose directional effects would otherwise be masked by sampling noise; by collapsing an extended body to a point, Newtonian mechanics isolates the dependence of orbital trajectories on total mass and center-of-mass separation. In each case, the factors removed are precisely those that, within the explanatory question being asked, do not make a difference to the outcome. Idealization, so understood, is a diagnostic tool for difference-makers: what can be falsified without disturbing the explanandum was never doing explanatory work to begin with, and what cannot be so falsified is thereby revealed as essential.

This diagnostic function connects naturally to a broader conception of what understanding a phenomenon amounts to. To understand why something occurs is to grasp how it would have been different had the relevant conditions been otherwise—to command a map of counterfactual dependencies linking variations in the underlying factors to variations in the outcome. On this view, understanding is not a matter of possessing a literally true description of a system but of possessing a representation that correctly tracks the pattern of what-if-things-had-been-otherwise relations the system actually exhibits. An idealized model can discharge this task superbly even while making assumptions known to be false, because the counterfactual structure it encodes can match the counterfactual structure of the target system in the respects that matter.
